name: Web Data Collection
title: Web Data Collection
answer: Web data collection is the practice of gathering information from public websites and web services at scale, usually by automated means, to build datasets that feed research, analytics and machine learning. In alternative data it covers everything from scraping product prices and job postings to pulling filings, reviews and shipping records. The output is typically a structured table or feed that can be joined to financial or operational data. It sits between data engineering and market research, and it is one of the most common ways alternative data firms build a raw signal.

sections.body: Web data collection is the practice of gathering information from public websites and web services at scale, usually by automated means, to build datasets that feed research, analytics and machine learning. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a stack of crawlers, schedulers and storage. Common tools include Python libraries such as Scrapy, BeautifulSoup and Playwright, headless browsers for pages that render with JavaScript, and proxy pools or rotating IPs to spread request load. Collected pages land in object storage or a database, then move through parsing and normalisation jobs. Larger operations add queueing systems, retry logic and monitoring so that a broken selector or a blocked route is noticed quickly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline starts with a target list of sites and the fields wanted from each. Crawlers fetch pages, parsers extract the fields, and validation checks catch missing or malformed records. Because sites change, teams maintain selector maps, version their parsers and keep raw snapshots so a parse can be rerun without refetching. Deduplication, entity matching and timestamping turn the raw captures into a usable panel. Quality control usually compares a sample of scraped values against the live page by hand.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The legal and ethical picture is layered. Terms of service, robots.txt, copyright, database rights, computer misuse statutes and data protection law such as the GDPR all bear on what may be collected and kept, and the answers differ by jurisdiction and by whether the data is personal. Public availability does not by itself settle the question. Good practice includes recording provenance for every record, honouring rate limits, avoiding personal data where it is not needed, and keeping an audit trail of what was fetched, when and from where. This page describes practice and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Collection is shifting toward APIs, licensed feeds and partnerships as sites harden against scraping and courts test the boundaries. Browser automation and residential proxy networks are becoming more common, which raises the cost and the compliance burden. Buyers increasingly ask for provenance and consent documentation alongside the data itself. Expect more emphasis on first party and permissioned sources, and on tooling that can prove where a number came from.
